title: I taught Ephraim to walk (Hosea 11:1–4)
hookLine: God as a parent holding a toddler's hands, bending down to feed

lines: ONE FINGER IN EACH TINY FIST.
THE CHILD THINKS THEY'RE WALKING ALONE.
cards: Watch a parent teach a toddler to walk. They crouch behind the child, one finger in each tiny fist, bent nearly double, back aching.
The child has no idea anyone is holding on, thinks they're walking all alone, and that's the point. Later, the same parent leans down with a spoon, patient, while half of it lands on the floor.
Somebody probably held each of us like that once, and nobody remembers it. An old prophet named Hosea reached for exactly this picture of God. Not a king on a throne.
A parent on their knees in the hallway.

teach.b: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel, and his book often calls the north Ephraim, after one of its tribes. In the King James Bible: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt."

teach.h: OUT OF EGYPT: A PARENT CALLING HOME.
teach.b: The Exodus, remembered not as a battle but as a parent calling a child home. Then the toddler scene: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them."
That's the ache: held, fed and healed, and never noticed.

teach.h: CORDS OF A MAN, BANDS OF LOVE.
teach.b: Verse four: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love." Not chains for an animal. Human cords, the kind a person uses to guide someone they love.

Then a farmer's picture: God easing the yoke off their jaws and bending down to lay food before them. The chapter isn't sweet all the way through. Hosea names the people's turning away, and hard years coming.
But a few verses later God says, in effect, my heart is turned within me; I can't give you up. The love outlasts the anger.

teach.h: I TAUGHT EPHRAIM ALSO TO GO.
teach.b: Matthew's Gospel later borrows the first line, out of Egypt have I called my son, and hears it in the child Jesus and his family in Egypt.
Christians who follow Matthew hear Hosea on two levels: Israel's story, and a pattern Jesus walks again. Either way, God in this book is the one on their knees.

how: Christians read Hosea 11 in sermons and Bible study as a picture of God's parental love, and Matthew 2:15 quotes its first verse in the story of Jesus' childhood.

o: love, the cords God used to draw a people
a yoke laid on an animal's neck for work
the old name of Israel's northern kingdom

games.q: what's inside Hosea 11 — tap the pairs.
p: a name for the northern kingdom
a parent calling a child home

s: in Hosea 11, the child knows who is holding them up
"they knew not that I healed them." the ache of the chapter is that the child never noticed.
the King James Bible says "I taught Ephraim also to go"
"to go" is the old English way of saying to walk.
Hosea 11 is gentle from start to finish
it also names the people's turning away and the hard years coming. the love outlasts the anger.

games.q: you're the parent in Hosea's picture. the child you taught to walk has wandered off and forgotten you. what does the chapter say happens to your heart?
o: it hardens, and you let them go.
it turns within you, and you can't give them up.
games.why: a few verses later, God says in effect: my heart is turned within me; how can I give you up? the love outlasts the anger.

practice: Picture the hands of someone who held you up before you could stand, even if you don't remember it; Hosea's point is that you probably wouldn't.
Then think of a small one in your life now, a child, a pet, a seedling, a younger colleague finding their feet, and one small act of care you could give them.
If you pray, give thanks for the hands that held you; if not, simply let the gratitude sit.

wordCard.voice: Ahavah. Hebrew for love: the cords Hosea says God used to draw a people, like a parent holding a toddler's arms, feeding them, healing them unseen.

orig.note: Hebrew: love. Hosea's "bands of love" are literally cords of ahavah.

carryVoice: Your line: cords of love. Most of the holding goes unseen, even by the one being held. Until tomorrow.
